title: Brokers, Prop Firms & Accounts
hook: Know the difference before you fund an account.

launchpad.outcome: Explain what a broker account, a prop firm evaluation, and a simulated account each actually test.
launchpad.missionQuestion: If you want to prove you're consistent before risking real money, which account type actually answers that?

slides.headline: Whose money is it?
slides.line: Every account is your money, someone else’s, or practice money.

cards.label: Broker account
cards.sub: Your own capital. Keep every profit, absorb every loss.

cards.label: Prop firm evaluation
cards.sub: Their capital, if you prove you can trade their rules.

cards.label: Simulated account
cards.sub: No real money. Pure practice, zero financial risk.

slides.kicker: Match the account to the goal
slides.headline: Prove it before real money.
slides.line: You want to test whether your execution is consistent before risking real money.

options.label: Jump straight to a funded account
options.feedback: Skipping straight to funded capital without proving consistency first is a real risk.

options.label: A simulated (demo) account
options.why: Right. Simulated accounts exist to prove consistency with zero financial risk.

slides.line: I’m not telling you which account type to start with. Know what that account expects from you before you place a single trade.

slides.headline: They passed. They’re funded.
slides.line: A trader passes a prop firm’s evaluation and gets funded.

check.prompt: Whose capital are they trading now?

options.label: Their own, the eval was a formality
options.feedback: The whole point of an evaluation is that it isn’t a formality. It decides whether they trade their own money or the firm’s.

options.label: Nobody’s, funded accounts are simulated
options.feedback: A funded account trades the firm’s real capital, not a simulation.

options.label: The firm’s, inside the firm’s rules
options.why: Their personal money isn’t directly at risk, but they now trade inside the firm’s rules. Funded status shifts whose money is at risk, and adds real rule constraints in exchange.

slides.prompt: Should you go straight for a funded prop account? Why or why not?
slides.modelAnswer: A funded prop account means trading someone else’s capital under their rules, without having proven yet that your execution is consistent. Going straight there skips the step where a simulated account lets you prove consistency with zero financial risk first, and most people fail an evaluation not because they don’t know the market, but because they haven’t proven their own discipline yet.

takeaways: A broker account risks your own capital from trade one.
A prop evaluation tests rule-discipline before granting capital access.
A simulated account proves consistency with zero financial risk.
remember: Know exactly which account you're in, and what it expects from you.
